article_title: A new criterion for assessing discriminant validity in variance-based structural equation modeling
citation: Henseler, J., Ringle, C. M., & Sarstedt, M. (2015). A new criterion for assessing discriminant validity in variance-based structural equation modeling. J. of the Acad. Mark. Sci. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11747-014-0403-8
title: Heterotrait-monotrait ratio (HTMT) of correlations as a discriminant validity criterion
description: The HTMT is a ratio derived from the multitrait-multimethod matrix: "the average of the heterotrait-heteromethod correlations" (correlations of indicators across constructs) "relative to the average of the monotrait-heteromethod correlations" (correlations of indicators within the same construct), with the geometric mean taken of the two within-construct averages. It estimates the correlation between two constructs without requiring factor analysis or construct scores, so it can be computed from a correlation matrix alone. It can be applied as a criterion against a threshold (0.85 or 0.90) or as a bootstrap-based statistical test (HTMT inference) with Bonferroni adjustment.
requirements: At least two reflectively measured constructs measured with multiple indicators from the same respondents
For HTMT inference, bootstrapping to construct confidence intervals and Bonferroni adjustment for multiple construct pairs
constraints: The HTMT-based criteria assume reflectively measured constructs; applying them to formatively measured constructs is problematic because neither monotrait-heteromethod nor heterotrait-heteromethod correlations of formative indicators are indicative of discriminant validity
target_learners: Researchers and practitioners using variance-based SEM in marketing and other social sciences disciplines
target_learning_goals: Correct assessment of discriminant validity as part of measurement model evaluation in variance-based SEM
examples: In the ACSI empirical example (N = 10,417), HTMT values ranged from 0.53 to 0.95, with HTMT.85 flagging two construct pairs and HTMT.90 one
key_sources: Henseler, J., Ringle, C. M., & Sarstedt, M. (2015). A new criterion for assessing discriminant validity in variance-based structural equation modeling. J. of the Acad. Mark. Sci. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11747-014-0403-8

article_title: The development of self-regulation across early childhood.
citation: Montroy Janelle J., Bowles Ryan P., Skibbe Lori E., McClelland Megan M., Morrison Frederick J. (2016). The Development of Self-Regulation across Early Childhood. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000159
title: Head-Toes-Knees-Shoulders (HTKS) task for assessing early childhood behavioral self-regulation
description: The HTKS is a direct assessment of behavioral self-regulation for children ages three to seven. "The HTKS is a short, game-like task where children are asked to 'do the opposite' in regards to a set of paired rules", tapping attention, working memory, and inhibition. Scores range from 0–40, with two points for correct responses and one for self-corrections. The article reports strong reliability (Cronbach's alpha .85–.94 across samples) and validity evidence, and notes growth in HTKS performance does not appear to be a function of practice effects.
requirements: Administered by trained research assistants in a quiet setting; children responding correctly to four or more of the first ten items receive the ten additional two-rule items
constraints: In the first year of the Michigan longitudinal sample only the first half was administered, requiring Rasch-based extrapolation to the full 40-item score
target_learners: children ages three to seven in preschool through early elementary school
examples: Used across all three samples with up to eight measurement occasions per child between preschool and first grade
key_sources: Montroy Janelle J., Bowles Ryan P., Skibbe Lori E., McClelland Megan M., Morrison Frederick J. (2016). The Development of Self-Regulation across Early Childhood. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000159

article_title: The application of human reliability analysis to carpal tunnel decompression.
citation: Lucey Á, Kennedy S, Hussey A, McInerney N, Kelly JL, Joyce KM. (2024). The application of human reliability analysis to carpal tunnel decompression. Ann R Coll Surg Engl. https://doi.org/10.1308/rcsann.2023.0038
title: Human reliability analysis via HTA and SHERPA as a framework for identifying error-prone steps in surgical skills acquisition
description: Human reliability analysis (HRA) is a structured approach that identifies systematically the impact of human error on a system to reduce adverse events. It combines hierarchical task analysis (HTA), the systematic decomposition of a procedure into component steps with focus on human factors, with SHERPA, which "identifies credible errors in a process and suggests methods of error mitigation at each step." HTA serves as the framework for applying SHERPA. The article applies this framework to carpal tunnel decompression to show trainees the sequential tasks, highlight error-prone steps and alert them to high-criticality steps.
requirements: Requires an optimum, standardised technique for the procedure, achieved through the iterative HTA process of literature review, observation and subject matter expert consensus
constraints: The article states it is difficult to apply HRA to emergency procedures or complex, major cases where surgical variation can be high and patient factors can play a large role
target_learners: trainee surgeons learning carpal tunnel decompression and comparable elective procedures
target_learning_goals: safe, error-reduced acquisition of operative technique; identification of high-risk and high-criticality procedural steps
examples: The framework was applied to carpal tunnel decompression using 20 observed procedures, a literature review, and five consultant plastic surgeon subject matter experts, producing 13 principal tasks, 46 subtasks and remedial strategies for each identified error.
key_sources: Lucey Á, Kennedy S, Hussey A, McInerney N, Kelly JL, Joyce KM. (2024). The application of human reliability analysis to carpal tunnel decompression. Ann R Coll Surg Engl. https://doi.org/10.1308/rcsann.2023.0038
